source_refs.note: 'Difference Between Prediction and Causation' under topic 6.9, as printed (PDF 88, printed 84).

blocks.text: Prediction estimates what may happen based on historical data. It focuses on forecasting outcomes, where the model uses past information to estimate future values or events. For example, a model may predict a student's final grade by analysing previous marks, attendance, and study hours. Similarly, a weather model may predict tomorrow's temperature by using past weather records. A model can make accurate predictions without necessarily understanding the underlying causes. This makes prediction useful in areas such as sales forecasting, stock trend analysis, disease risk prediction, and student performance estimation.

Causation, on the other hand, explains why something happens by identifying cause-and-effect relationships between variables. It seeks to uncover the reasons behind events and how one factor directly influences another. For example, if regular study hours directly improve exam performance, then study time may be considered a cause of better grades. Similarly, if smoking directly increases the risk of lung disease, this shows a causal relationship. Understanding causality is important for decision-making because it helps avoid false assumptions and provides deeper insight into real-world problems.
